Dermatology · published research

Chemotherapy-induced alopecia

One small trial reported a short-term hair-growth difference after chemotherapy, while another found no added prevention benefit on scalp coverage or hair thickness when PBM was combined with scalp cooling. Quality-of-life results differed by outcome.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small trial reported a short-term hair-growth difference after chemotherapy, while another found no added prevention benefit on scalp coverage or hair thickness when PBM was combined with scalp cooling. Quality-of-life results differed by outcome.

Summary of the Evidence

Five publications address chemotherapy-induced alopecia: two small randomized trials with 32 and 29 participants, one trial protocol, one commentary, and one rat study. The commentary is not an independent cohort, and the protocol contributes no outcome results. The two human trials address different questions: regrowth after chemotherapy versus prevention during chemotherapy with scalp cooling.

Human and clinical evidence

The HAIRLASER trial randomized 32 breast-cancer patients after anthracycline- and taxane-containing chemotherapy to PBM or no intervention. Treatment began on the final chemotherapy day and involved three sessions weekly for 12 weeks. Blinded reviewers found a higher hair-growth score in the PBM group at one month, but that difference was not maintained at months two and three. Global-health scores were higher in the PBM group at the reported assessment points (Lodewijckx et al. 2023). A separate 29-person randomized trial added PBM to scalp cooling to prevent hair loss. It did not find significant differences in scalp coverage or hair thickness, although some quality-of-life domains favored the add-on group (Tripathi et al. 2025). The trials are small and their outcomes should not be combined as one treatment effect.

Animal evidence

One rat chemotherapy model reported faster hair regrowth after light exposure and did not find that the intervention reduced the antitumor effect of the chemotherapy used in that model. This is a preclinical safety and regrowth observation, not evidence of effectiveness or oncologic safety in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No indication-specific cell or tissue study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The HAIRLASER abstract specifies three sessions per week for 12 weeks beginning on the last chemotherapy day, but does not give enough wavelength and dose detail to compare exposure with other protocols. The prevention trial tested PBM alongside scalp cooling and therefore cannot be read as a stand-alone PBM prevention study. The source record for the rat experiment describes red light, but animal delivery and dose do not establish a human protocol. No comparative dose-finding study was identified.

Interpretation

The post-chemotherapy trial reports a hair-growth difference at one month that was not maintained at later measurements; the prevention trial did not show added benefit on its scalp-coverage or hair-thickness outcomes. These are distinct uses of PBM. Current human evidence does not establish reliable prevention or durable regrowth, while the quality-of-life findings merit separate, adequately powered replication.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term hair regrowth after chemotherapy Very low for prevention when PBM is added to scalp cooling
Publications and records5 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small randomized trials address different questions. One reports a higher hair-growth score at one month after chemotherapy but not at later follow-ups; the other found no significant improvement in scalp coverage or hair thickness when PBM was added to cooling. Larger trials with consistent schedules, blinded assessment, and follow-up would clarify each use separately.
